note: The world's largest island, home to mostly Inuit Greenlanders; it controls its own affairs while Denmark handles defense and foreign policy.
A Caribbean island under the US flag since 1898; Puerto Ricans are US citizens with their own culture, baseball stars and booming music scene.
A former British colony handed back to China in 1997; it runs its own capitalist system under One Country, Two Systems.
A self-governing island that China claims as its own; Taiwan built an Asian democracy and a tech powerhouse of its own.
A state recognized by over 130 countries, governing Palestinian lands in the West Bank and Gaza amid a long conflict with Israel.
A North Atlantic archipelago of 18 volcanic islands with its own language; it governs itself while staying part of the Danish realm.
A tiny peninsula Spain ceded to Britain in 1713; its famous Rock guards the entrance to the Mediterranean.
A Celtic island in the Irish Sea with its own parliament, Tynwald, said to be over a thousand years old.
The largest Channel Island, loyal to the English Crown since Norman times, just off the French coast.
A Channel Island with a trading past and its own government; smaller sister islands Sark and Alderney sit nearby.
South Atlantic islands claimed by both Britain and Argentina; they fought a short war over them in 1982 and Britain holds them today.
A wealthy Atlantic island settled by the English in 1612, famous for shipwrecks, pastel houses and triangles of mystery.
A Caribbean finance hub discovered by Columbus in 1503; turtles and pirates came first, banks came later.
A yacht-lover's paradise of Caribbean islands named by Columbus after Saint Ursula's 11,000 virgins.
A quiet coral Caribbean island, Britain's first colony in the region, now known for reefs and relaxed luxury.
Half the island was buried by its volcano in 1995; the old capital is a modern Pompeii.
A chain of low-lying Caribbean islands whose salt pans once made fortunes; today its beaches top world rankings.
Three ultra-remote Atlantic islands; Napoleon died on St Helena in 1821, and Tristan da Cunha is the world's most isolated settlement.
France's subantarctic lands, some of the most remote and storm-battered islands on Earth.
The place where Ernest Shackleton reached rescue in 1916 after one of history's greatest survival journeys.
A central Indian Ocean atoll chain; the largest island hosts a major UK-US military base, and its native islanders were relocated in the 1960s-70s.
An Australian island settled by descendants of HMS Bounty mutineers, who still speak a Creole language from Tahiti and old English.
An Indian Ocean island famous for its millions of red crabs marching to the sea each November.
Two atolls southwest of Java with a Malay-majority community and superb untouched reefs.
A French Pacific territory with a huge reef lagoon and a strong indigenous Kanak identity, easing toward possible independence.
France's Polynesian paradise of 118 islands, once the site of French nuclear tests, now living on tourism and black pearls.
Three Polynesian islands under the French flag where local kings still share power with French authority.
A French Caribbean island that is legally as French as Paris, with EU euros, croissants and rum distilleries.
A French island in the Caribbean whose volcano destroyed its capital Saint-Pierre in 1902 in minutes.
A volcanic French island near Madagascar where lava flows, mountain cirques and Creole culture meet.

famous: one of the world's largest lagoons
note: A French island between Madagascar and Mozambique, claimed also by Comoros, ringed by a stunning reef.
A tiny French-Swedish-flavored celebrity island in the Caribbean where yachts and baguettes mix.
The north half of a Caribbean island shared with the Netherlands; the world's smallest land split between two nations.
Eight tiny islands south of Newfoundland that stayed French after Britain took Canada; locals still speak Norman French.
The world's smallest country, a 0.5 km² enclave in Rome, seat of the Pope and the Catholic Church since 1929.
A tiny Mediterranean principality ruled by the Grimaldi dynasty for 700+ years, famed for luxury and racing.
Founded in AD 301 by a saint, San Marino claims to be the world's oldest surviving republic.
A Pyrenean state whose heads of state are, to this day, the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell in Spain.
A German-speaking Alpine principality ruled by the House of Liechtenstein, once nearly mistaken for Czechia on a map in 2013... actually a famous Swiss army exercise invaded it by mistake.
An island nation crossed by every Mediterranean empire, ruled famously by crusading Knights, now the EU's smallest member.
A tiny Pacific island that got rich then poor mining phosphate, and once had the world's highest obesity rates.
One of the smallest and most remote countries, on the front line of rising seas it did little to cause.
A Pacific nation of 340 islands with shark sanctuaries and a lake where you can swim with stingless jellyfish.
A scattered Pacific nation where the US tested 60+ nuclear bombs, including one larger than 1,000 Hiroshimas.
The smallest nation in the Americas; St Kitts and Nevis were sugar islands where Britain and France dueled for centuries.
An Antiguan-Barbudan twin-island nation whose English Harbour once sheltered Admiral Nelson's fleet.
A green mountainous island still home to indigenous Kalinago people, the last in the Caribbean.
The Spice Isle whose flag features a nutmeg; the US briefly invaded it in 1983 during a Cold War power struggle.
A Caribbean island that switched between French and British rule 14 times, keeping both Creole and cricket.
A nation of 32 islands and cays where sailors island-hop between some of the Caribbean's best waters.
A coral island that kept British institutions after 1966 independence and became a republic in 2021, home of Rihanna.

famous: the granite boulders of La Digue
note: A 115-island Indian Ocean nation, once a pirate hideout and later the playground of the rich.
Three islands that broke from France in 1975; the fourth, Mayotte, stayed French and is still disputed.
Two former Portuguese slave-and-cocoa islands near the equator, Africa's second-smallest country.
Ten volcanic Atlantic islands off Senegal, uninhabited until the Portuguese arrived in 1456, now a stable democracy.
A South Pacific territory under the US flag since 1900, holding some of the world's last communal land systems.
Caribbean islands Denmark sold to the US in 1917 for $25 million, fearing German U-boats.
A Pacific island seized from Spain in 1898; Chamorro people have lived there for 4,000 years.
Northern Mariana islands that went from Spanish to German to Japanese to American rule over one century.
A Dutch Caribbean island famous for its pastel colonial capital, a UNESCO site, and the liqueur named after it.
A Dutch island outside the hurricane belt, with one of the Caribbean's most visited beaches.
The Dutch south half of St Martin island, sharing the smallest divided island in the world with France.
The Caribbean Netherlands: Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, islands that became direct Dutch municipalities in 2010.
A Swedish-speaking Finnish archipelago demilitarized by international treaty in 1921.
Norwegian Arctic islands where it is illegal to die (seriously, for practical reasons) and the world stores backup seeds.
Cook Islanders hold New Zealand citizenship and run their own affairs in free association with Wellington.
A piece of France on the South American mainland that launches Europe’s rockets from Kourou.

famous: one of the world’s smallest democracies
note: A tiny raised coral atoll nation of about 1,600 people associated with New Zealand.
Three remote atolls whose people were brought to New Zealand in the 19th century, now self-governing under Wellington.
A breakaway province of Serbia that declared independence in 2008; many countries recognize Kosovo, Serbia and others do not.

famous: one of the most isolated communities on Earth
note: Fifty or so islanders, mostly descended from the 1789 Bounty mutineers, live on one of the most remote islands on the planet.
A desert territory mostly administered by Morocco after Spain left in 1975; the local Sahrawi republic is partially recognized.
